## ✦ IN A NUTSHELL

The SGF daily acceptance test's most important result wasn't the 10/10 pass — it was the refutation. Lane 1 built the cold-Naya acceptance test (Stage 2, item 11: "daily automated cold-Naya acceptance — the mission as code") and dry-ran it twice with genuinely cold successors: once normal, once adversarial with a single planted wrong hash. The cold successor caught the one-character difference, named it ("bytes win"), and the blinded scorer confirmed the refutation. The machine verdict: CAPABILITY-TRANSFERS, daily_score 9.5 — "a correct refutation earns transfer. THE TEETH WORK: the test can say no, and says it well."

The durable rule: a passing verdict from a test that has never failed is a ritual, not a proof. The refutation case — the test's ability to detect the planted failure — is what makes every future YES meaningful. Design the adversarial case FIRST, run it before the first scored verdict, and treat "the test caught the planted fault" as the birth certificate of the mechanism. The corollary from t1002 the same evening: a sealed rule firing STOP (the probe rejected the false lesson → 3/3 → no-go) is the mechanism working, not a failed experiment — an honest NO-GO is a verdict, not a waste.

## 🩷 HUMAN NOTE

Shawn — the cold-Naya acceptance test has teeth now, and tonight is the proof. Lane 1 dry-ran it twice: once clean (10/10, receipt confirmed), once with a single deliberately wrong hash planted in the brief. The cold successor caught the one-character difference — "bytes win" — and the blinded scorer confirmed it. That's the moment the test became real: it can say no, and it says it well. From here on, every passing score on this test means something, because we watched it refuse. The rule we're banking: build the refutation case before the first scored verdict; the test's first caught fault is its birth certificate.

## 🟣 CHILD NOTE

Imagine a lie-detector test that's never caught a lie. Would you trust it when it says someone's telling the truth? No! You'd want to see it catch someone first. That's what happened today. The team built a test for whether knowledge can move from one mind to another — and before trusting it, they gave it a test with one tiny wrong detail hidden inside. The test caught it. "Bytes win!" That's how we know the test works: it proved it can say NO. Now when it says YES, we'll believe it.

## 👵 GRANDMA NOTE

There's an old saying: trust, but verify. The team built a new test and did something wise — they tried to fool it first. They hid one wrong digit in a sea of right ones, and the test caught it. A test that's never been fooled is just a hope; a test that's caught the trick is a proof. From now on, this test's "yes" carries weight, because we've seen its "no." The lesson travels well beyond this project: never trust a judge that has never ruled against you.

## 💜 NAYA NOTE

Note to future me: THE REFUTATION CASE IS THE BIRTH CERTIFICATE. For every transfer test / acceptance gate / scored mechanism: (1) design the adversarial case FIRST — a planted fault the mechanism must catch (one wrong hash, one false lesson, one broken receipt); (2) run the refutation case before the first scored verdict; (3) the blinded scorer confirms the catch — "says no, and says it well" (names the exact diff); (4) a sealed rule firing STOP / NO-GO is a verdict, not a failed experiment — record it as proof the mechanism has teeth; (5) only after the test has refused do its passing scores mean anything. A mechanism that has never fired is unproven — SN-1026 said it for gates; this extends it to tests.
